terms.grammar: pronoun: the ordinary forms of ego, used reflexively
evidence: Cic. Att. 8.14.2: ego tēcum tamquam mēcum loquor
terms.comment: Latin has no separate reflexive for the first person: “I wash myself” is mē lavō, “with myself” mēcum. Many English reflexives are a plain verb in Latin: “I enjoy myself”, mē oblectō or simply gaudeō.

terms.gloss: myself (for emphasis: I myself, in person)
terms.grammar: pronoun, intensive: genitive ipsīus, dative ipsī
evidence: Plin. NH 8.6: ipse ego haec scrīpsī
Cic. Amic. 10: mē ipse cōnsōlor (Lewis & Short, s.v. ipse, Lael. 3.10)
terms.comment: The “myself” of “I did it myself”: it agrees with ego, said or understood (ipse for a man, ipsa for a woman). With a reflexive, ipse in the nominative stresses the doer: mē ipse cōnsōlor, I console myself (no one else does).

evidence: Mart. 14.73.2: hoc didicī per mē dīcere

phrases.english: I talk to you as if I were talking to myself.

phrases.latin: sed nōn egeō medicīnā: mē ipse cōnsōlor
phrases.english: But I need no medicine: I console myself.

phrases.latin: vix mī ipse crēdēns Thȳniam atque Bīthȳnōs līquisse campōs et vidēre tē in tūtō
phrases.english: hardly believing myself that I have left Thynia and the plains of Bithynia, and that I see you in safety

phrases.latin: ego ipsa sum, inquit, hīc hospita
phrases.english: “I’m only a guest here myself,” she said.

phrases.latin: nōn enim concēdō tibi plūs ut illum amēs quam ipse amō
phrases.english: For I won’t grant that you love him more than I do myself.

phrases.latin: ipse ego haec scrīpsī et spolia Celtica dicāvī
phrases.english: I wrote this myself and dedicated the Celtic spoils.

phrases.latin: psittacus ā vōbīs aliōrum nōmina discam: hoc didicī per mē dīcere "Caesar, havē"
phrases.english: The parrot: I shall learn other names from you; this I learned to say by myself: “Hail, Caesar!”
